items.q: As a smooth vertical wall moves away from the soil it retains, the horizontal effective stress on the wall

options.A: falls from the at-rest value K₀σ′<sub>v</sub> to the active value K<sub>a</sub>σ′<sub>v</sub>
options.C: becomes equal to the vertical stress

items.why: Lateral expansion lets the soil mobilise its shear strength, so the horizontal stress drops until the soil is at the point of failure (active state).

items.q: For φ′ = 30° the Rankine coefficients are
Jaky's K₀ = 1 − sinφ′ for a normally consolidated sand with φ′ = 30° is 0.5. For an over-consolidated clay with the same K₀(NC) and OCR = 4, K₀ = K₀(NC)·OCR<sup>0.5</sup> is
items.why: 0.5 × 4<sup>0.5</sup> = 0.5 × 2 = 1.0. Over-consolidation locks in horizontal stress.

items.q: Dry sand, γ = 18 kN/m³, φ′ = 30°, horizontal surface. The Rankine active pressure at 5 m depth is
items.why: p<sub>a</sub> = K<sub>a</sub>γz = (1/3)·18·5 = 30 kPa (K<sub>p</sub> would give 270).

items.q: The total active thrust on a 5 m wall in the same dry sand (γ = 18, φ′ = 30°) and the height at which it acts above the base are
items.why: P<sub>a</sub> = ½K<sub>a</sub>γH² = ½·(1/3)·18·25 = 75 kN/m. A triangular pressure acts at H/3 = 1.67 m above the base.

items.q: A uniform surcharge q on the surface adds to the active pressure
items.why: The vertical stress at every depth rises by q, so the horizontal pressure rises by K<sub>a</sub>q everywhere: a rectangle on the diagram.

items.q: Compared with the movement needed to reach the active state, the movement needed to mobilise full passive resistance is
items.why: Passive failure needs the soil to be compressed substantially; this is why walls rely on only part of the passive resistance.

items.q: Which is not an assumption of Rankine's theory?

options.A: The wall is smooth, so the stress on it is a principal stress
options.B: The soil is homogeneous and isotropic
options.C: Every point in the soil is on the verge of failure (Mohr–Coulomb)
options.D: The wall is rough, so shear stresses act on its back

items.why: A smooth wall carries no shear, which keeps vertical and horizontal stresses principal. Wall roughness belongs to Coulomb.

items.q: At the interface between two soils with different friction angles, the Rankine pressure diagram

options.A: jumps, because K<sub>a</sub> changes while the vertical stress does not

items.why: σ′<sub>v</sub> is continuous but K is not, so p = Kσ′<sub>v</sub> has a step. Compute the pressure just above and just below.

items.q: Sand φ′ = 35° (K<sub>a</sub> = 0.271), 5 m wall, γ = 17 kN/m³ above the water table, saturated 20 kN/m³ below. With the water table 2 m below the surface the total thrust (soil and water, g<sub>w</sub> = 9.81) is about
items.why: Soil above: ½·0.271·17·2² = 9.2; surcharge of that layer on the wet part: 0.271·17·2·3 = 27.6; submerged soil: ½·0.271·10.19·3² = 12.4; water: ½·9.81·3² = 44.1. Total 93.4 kN/m. Without the water table: 57.6 kN/m.

items.q: The water in the pores of the backfill

options.A: acts only on the passive side
options.B: reduces the thrust because soil weight is buoyant, and nothing is added
options.C: adds a hydrostatic thrust ½γ<sub>w</sub>h<sub>w</sub>² on top of the effective soil thrust

items.why: The soil part uses γ′ (smaller), but the pore pressure acts fully on the wall, so the total thrust is larger than the dry case.

items.q: Undrained analysis of a clay (φ<sub>u</sub> = 0): K<sub>a</sub> = 1 and p<sub>a</sub> = σ<sub>v</sub> − 2c<sub>u</sub>. At 6 m with γ = 18 kN/m³ and c<sub>u</sub> = 30 kPa the pressure is
items.why: σ<sub>v</sub> = 18·6 = 108 kPa; p<sub>a</sub> = 108 − 2·30 = 48 kPa (a total stress: no separate water pressure).

items.q: "Immediately after construction", a clay layer is analysed with

options.A: total stress and undrained strength c<sub>u</sub>, φ<sub>u</sub> = 0

items.why: Clay has not had time to drain, so excess pore pressures remain; the sand drains at once and is analysed in effective stress.

items.q: A clay with c<sub>u</sub> = 10 kPa, φ<sub>u</sub> = 0, γ = 18 kN/m³. The depth of the tension crack z₀ = 2c<sub>u</sub>/γ is
Tension cracks in the backfill can occur in

options.C: clays (cohesive soils), mainly in undrained conditions

items.why: Without cohesion the active pressure is positive from the surface; negative values (tension) need c.

items.q: The critical depth of an unsupported vertical cut in clay (φ<sub>u</sub> = 0) is H<sub>c</sub> = 4c<sub>u</sub>/γ. For c<sub>u</sub> = 30 kPa and γ = 18 kN/m³ it is
items.why: 4·30/18 = 6.67 m. This is twice the crack depth z₀ = 2c<sub>u</sub>/γ = 3.3 m.

items.q: If a tension crack fills with water, the thrust on the wall

options.A: rises by ½γ<sub>w</sub>z₀², which is the conservative design assumption
options.D: falls because water supports the soil

items.why: The water pressure acts on the wall over the crack depth and cannot be relied on to be absent.

items.q: The depth of the tension crack is the depth at which

options.B: the active pressure p<sub>a</sub> = K<sub>a</sub>γz − 2c′√K<sub>a</sub> becomes zero

items.why: z₀ = 2c′/(γ√K<sub>a</sub>). Above it the formula gives tension, which soil cannot carry.

items.q: For a sloping surface (angle β) in Rankine's theory, the active pressure acts

options.A: normal to the wall at δ
options.C: parallel to the slope, p<sub>a</sub> = K<sub>a</sub>γz cosβ

items.why: The lecture states the pressure on a vertical plane acts parallel to the surface, so P<sub>a</sub> = ½K<sub>a</sub>γH²cosβ with K<sub>a</sub> from the sloping-surface formula.

items.q: K<sub>a</sub> for φ′ = 40° and β = 20° is 0.266. For a 6 m wall, γ = 18 kN/m³, the thrust P<sub>a</sub> = ½K<sub>a</sub>γH²cosβ is about
Coulomb's theory differs from Rankine's because it

options.A: balances the forces on a trial soil wedge and allows wall friction and an inclined wall back
options.C: ignores the weight of the wedge
options.D: is exact for passive pressure with large δ

items.why: The wedge is in limiting equilibrium under its weight, the wall reaction at δ to the normal and the plane reaction at φ′. The maximum over trial planes is the active thrust.

items.q: Wall friction δ, compared with a smooth wall,

options.B: reduces the active thrust and increases the passive resistance

items.why: Friction on the wall helps carry the wedge, so the active thrust falls; in the passive case it adds resistance (but the failure surface curves).

items.q: Coulomb's plane-failure assumption for passive pressure

options.C: overestimates resistance for large δ (above about φ′/3), which is unsafe; use Caquot and Kerisel instead

items.why: The failure surface is clearly curved in the passive case; the lecture recommends Caquot–Kerisel or Sokolovski coefficients for larger δ.

items.q: Where does the Coulomb active thrust act on a vertical wall, relative to the wall normal?

options.D: at δ to the normal (so it has a vertical component)

items.why: The reaction P makes angle δ with the normal to the wall (below it for an active wedge that slides down). On a vertical wall the horizontal component is P cosδ.

items.q: A Coulomb thrust P<sub>a</sub> = 56.7 kN/m acts at δ = 15° to the horizontal on a vertical wall. Its horizontal component is
items.why: P<sub>a</sub>cosδ = 56.7·0.966 = 54.8 kN/m. The vertical part P<sub>a</sub>sinδ = 14.7 kN/m adds to the wall load.

items.q: In design, the mobilised friction angle is taken lower than the critical-state value φ<sub>cs</sub> because

options.B: loads and soil properties are uncertain, small wall rotations do not mobilise peak strength, and backfill can contain shear bands

items.why: Design values are conservative: uncertainty, tolerable rotation and construction quality (lecture list).

items.q: Embedded (sheet pile, secant pile, diaphragm) walls differ from gravity walls because they

options.A: are heavy and resist by weight
options.C: are flexural members whose weight is ignored and which depend on mobilised passive resistance

items.why: Excavation follows installation; stability comes from the embedded length and the passive resistance in front.

items.q: The three stability checks for a gravity retaining wall are

options.D: overturning, sliding and bearing capacity of the foundation soil

items.why: The thrust must not overturn the wall about the toe, slide it along the base, or exceed the bearing capacity (tutorial 12(ii) checks the pressure on the foundation against 250 kPa).

items.q: In the lecture's cantilever sheet pile example, two factors are used: 1.2 on the soil shear strength and 1.3 on the embedment. The aim is to

options.A: reduce the strength used in K<sub>a</sub>, K<sub>p</sub>, and then increase the calculated driving depth, so the wall is safe against rotation

items.why: Soil strength is divided by 1.2 before finding K<sub>a</sub> and K<sub>p</sub>; the embedment found for equilibrium is multiplied by 1.3 for the safe driving depth.

items.q: A good retaining wall design includes

options.A: no drainage, to keep the soil strong
options.B: a high-quality drainage system to keep water out of the backfill

items.why: Water pressure on the wall can double the thrust; drained granular backfill is the usual design.
